tagline: Where the Danube meets the Balkans
overview:
Serbia sits at the center of the Balkan Peninsula, a landlocked country about the size of South Carolina, with mountains in the south and the flat, fertile plains of Vojvodina in the north. The Danube crosses it from west to east, meets the Sava River at Belgrade, and then squeezes through the Iron Gates gorge on the Romanian border.

About 6.6 million people live in Serbia and speak Serbian, which is unusual for being written in two alphabets, Cyrillic and Latin. Belgrade, the capital, is one of the oldest cities in Europe, watched over by a fortress on the ridge above the meeting of the rivers. Serbia is a parliamentary republic and has applied to join the European Union.

Kosovo, formerly a province in southern Serbia, declared independence in 2008. Serbia does not recognize it, many countries do, and talks between the two sides have continued for years.
landAndNature: Northern Serbia belongs to the Pannonian Plain, a checkerboard of wheat, corn, and sunflower fields so level that the horizon seems to run on forever. South of the Danube the land climbs into hills and then mountains, reaching 2,169 meters at Midžor on the Bulgarian border, with the Dinaric ranges to the west. The Iron Gates, known in Serbian as Đerdap, form one of the longest and deepest river gorges in Europe, where the Danube narrows between cliffs. Oak and beech forests shelter wolves, bears, deer, and imperial eagles, while the Uvac canyon has become a stronghold for the griffon vulture, a bird whose wings can span nearly three meters.
peopleAndCulture: Most Serbs belong to the Serbian Orthodox Church, and each family honors a patron saint on a day called slava, when the house fills with guests, round bread, and boiled wheat. Hungarian, Bosniak, Roma, and other communities add their own traditions, especially in Vojvodina. Meals are generous: grilled ćevapi and pljeskavica, sarma cabbage rolls, ajvar pepper relish, and flaky burek for breakfast. Brass bands take over the town of Guča each summer for a trumpet festival where the music runs all night. Serbia produces outstanding athletes for its size, particularly in basketball, water polo, volleyball, and tennis, where Novak Djokovic became one of the greatest players in the sport's history.
history: Several Roman emperors, including Constantine the Great, were born in this region. Slavs settled in the 600s, and a medieval Serbian kingdom reached its height in the 1300s before Ottoman armies won the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 and eventually absorbed the land. Uprisings beginning in 1804 rebuilt Serbian self-rule, and full independence was recognized in 1878. The killing of an Austrian archduke in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered World War I, in which Serbia suffered enormous losses. Afterward it became the largest part of Yugoslavia. When Yugoslavia broke apart in the 1990s, wars in Croatia, Bosnia, and later Kosovo killed more than 100,000 people across the region, and NATO bombed Serbia in 1999. Montenegro left their union in 2006.
funFacts: Belgrade's fortress stands on a ridge that armies have fought over for roughly 2,000 years, and the city has been rebuilt dozens of times.
Nikola Tesla, whose ideas made alternating-current electricity practical, was an ethnic Serb; Belgrade's airport and a museum carry his name.
The Guča trumpet festival draws hundreds of thousands of visitors to a small Serbian town every summer.
Serbia is one of the world's leading raspberry growers, supplying a large share of the frozen raspberries sold worldwide.
Vinča, near Belgrade, was a farming settlement about 7,000 years ago that left behind clay figures with striking masked faces.
